subject: Chemistry
title: Why Bananas Ripen Other Fruit
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Bananas Ripen Other Fruit usable.

hook.text: Put a banana next to unripe avocados and they ripen faster. The banana releases an invisible gas.

buildup.text: The gas is ethylene—C₂H₄. It's a plant hormone that triggers the ripening process.

discovery.text: Ethylene signals fruit to convert starch into sugar, soften cell walls, and produce aroma compounds.

twist.text: The fruit industry uses this deliberately. Bananas are shipped green and gassed with ethylene at the destination.

climax.text: One bad apple really does spoil the barrel—damaged fruit produces extra ethylene, ripening everything nearby.

punchline.text: A tiny gas molecule tells fruit to ripen. One banana speeds them all.

quiz.question: What gas do bananas release that ripens nearby fruit?

details.summary: Bananas release ethylene gas, a plant hormone that signals surrounding fruit to begin ripening. Ethylene triggers enzymes that break down starches into sugars, soften cell walls, and produce aromatic compounds..
details.whyItMatters: Ethylene biology is critical to the global fruit supply chain. Understanding this chemical signal allows growers to control ripening during storage and shipping.
takeaways: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that triggers ripening enzymes
It converts starches to sugars and softens fruit cell walls
Commercial fruit is often shipped unripe and ripened with ethylene on arrival

faq.question: Why do bananas produce more ethylene than most other fruits?
faq.answer: Bananas are climacteric fruits that undergo a burst of ethylene production and cellular respiration during ripening. Their tropical origin and rapid post-harvest maturation cycle means they evolved to ripen quickly and signal nearby fruit. Apples and tomatoes also produce significant ethylene.

faq.question: Can you slow fruit ripening by removing ethylene from the air?
faq.answer: Yes. Commercial cold storage facilities use ethylene scrubbers and controlled atmosphere technology to remove ethylene and slow ripening. Potassium permanganate sachets absorb ethylene in shipping containers. This allows fruit to be stored for months longer than it would last naturally.
